Good evening, everyone. I run the interview program, so let me explain what actually happens after you apply. Most of our interviews are conducted by volunteer graduates of the college, people who live in or near your region and who give up an evening because they remember what it felt like to be seventeen. These days many of the conversations happen online. Now, the question I get most often is how much the interview counts. The honest answer is that it is one piece among many. It very rarely decides an application on its own. What it can do is add real color to a file, a sense of the person behind the grades and the essays. I read hundreds of interview reports every year, and I can tell you what the strongest ones say. They almost never say the applicant was impressive. They say something like, I would happily have kept talking for another hour. And very often they add that the student asked the interviewer a genuine question, and actually listened to the answer.

So my interview was in a coffee shop, and it was going fine until the interviewer asked, what book changed your mind about something? And I froze. My brain just started listing famous books I thought would sound impressive, and I actually began to talk about one I had only half read. About twenty seconds in, I could see in her face that she knew. So I stopped. I said, sorry, that is a really good question, can I have a second to think? And she said, of course. And then I told her the truth, which was that the book that changed my mind was a comic book about a family of immigrants, and it made me stop being embarrassed about my grandparents' accent. We talked about that for fifteen minutes. I found out later that she was the daughter of immigrants herself. What I learned is that a pause you actually name sounds much more confident than a rehearsed answer, and that telling the truth is what turned the interview into a conversation.
